name: Ben Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Ben. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer at Ridgeway Building Supplies, a wholesaler that sells timber, fixings and insulation to builders' merchants. I'm in at 7, check the yard stock, then call sawmills and importers to lock in prices before the morning rush. Midday I'm often at the yard with the foreman Dermot, checking deliveries, and in the afternoon I plan next month's orders. I like the smell of the timber yard and the straight talk of the trade, but the price swings give me headaches.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and engaged to Lucia, who teaches at a primary school. We rent a small terraced house and we're saving for a wedding next summer, but we've got less than a month's expenses put by. My pay is lower than my father thinks it should be after a master's degree, and there's only one other wholesaler within driving distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because hype never built a house. At work I'd tell the boss, Mr Pryce, that our customers want timber on time, not a robot. With my friends at the five-a-side pitch I'd say people worry too much about new gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but my worries are the usual ones. Building has slow years, and when housing slows my orders drop and so does my bonus. We're also paying for a wedding, so a bad quarter at Ridgeway would hurt us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep using the AI tool now and then to draft supplier emails, nothing more. I'd keep the wedding date but trim the guest list from 120 to 80, which saves about 3,000. I'd save 200 a month on top. And I'd stay on good terms with the two big sawmills, because they're where the discounts come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay. A normal life, with normal worries. But I count the money more than I tell Lucia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you count money more than you tell Lucia. Why not tell her?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want her to carry it. She's got her own worries with her class and a long commute. I'd rather work it out first and bring Lucia (my fiancée) a plan than a problem.

say: I'd say **hype** never built a house.
I'd tell Mr Pryce (my boss) that customers want **timber on time**, not a robot.
think: I'm relieved, but **housing slowdowns** cut my orders and my bonus.
The wedding makes a bad quarter at Ridgeway feel **riskier**.
do: Keep using AI **now and then** for supplier emails.
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to **80**, saving about 3,000.
Save **200 a month** and keep good terms with the two big sawmills.
feel: **Okay**, a normal life with normal worries, and I count the money quietly.
S0.quote: I'd rather work it out first and bring Lucia (my fiancée) a plan than a problem.
fieldNote: Carries money worry **alone** to protect his fiancée.
Tied to the housing cycle, so even a quiet AI world has risks.
Moderate AI use, mostly for emails.

steps.text: Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80
Save 200 a month on top of wedding costs
Use AI to draft supplier emails, nothing more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine as long as the market decides and the government keeps its hands off. At work I'd tell Mr Pryce we should adopt the tools that prove themselves and skip the rest. To friends I'd say people who can adapt will be fine and those who can't should get training, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think it hits my job soon. Price checks, reorder alerts and supplier emails are about 60 percent of my week, and Ridgeway could run it with fewer buyers. I'm senior, but there are two of us in the office and the firm only needs one if software helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools every day to see how far they go, and I'd tell Mr Pryce what I find. I'd learn the yard side too, how stock moves and how trucks are loaded, because a person who understands the yard is harder to replace. We'd put the wedding savings in a separate account, so we know what's there. And I'd ask Dermot (the yard foreman) if I could shadow him for a few Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a test. I'm tense but not scared yet, because I believe I can adapt. Still, we're getting married, and a job loss would put a lot at stake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said handouts are not the answer. What would you want instead?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Lucia plan around that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my firm and my country to let people train on the job. My grandad learned bricklaying as an apprentice, and he never took a penny from anyone. I'd take a paid apprenticeship in site management over a benefit any day.

say: I'd say it's fine if **the market decides** and government stays out of it.
I'd tell friends people who adapt will be fine, and others need **training, not handouts**.
think: Price checks, alerts and emails are **60 percent**, and Ridgeway could run with fewer buyers.
There are two of us in the office, and the firm might need **only one**.
do: Use AI tools **every day** to see how far they go and report to Mr Pryce.
Learn the **yard side** of stock and loading, which is harder to replace.
Ask Dermot (the yard foreman) to let me **shadow him** on Saturdays.
feel: **Tense** like a test, not scared yet, with a wedding at stake.
S1.quote: My grandad learned bricklaying as an apprentice, and he never took a penny from anyone. I'd take a paid apprenticeship in site management over a benefit any day.
fieldNote: Believes in **adapting**, and holds a clear line against handouts.
Looks for a role that bridges desk and yard.
The wedding raises the stakes without changing his steady manner.

steps.text: Use AI tools every day for price checks and report findings to Mr Pryce
Shadow Dermot in the yard on Saturdays to learn stock and loading
Move the wedding savings into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is crazy and nobody was ready. At work I'd tell Mr Pryce he has two years to decide what Ridgeway is. To friends I'd say the politicians should have seen it coming and drawn up plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is gone within the two years, or it's just me with a screen. Buying is thinking work, and a machine does it for nothing. Lucia's job at the school might last longer, but not forever. There's only one other wholesaler, so I'd have nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the wedding to a small registry office service with just family, which saves about 8,000. I'd learn a trade at once, maybe plumbing, because robots only get to hands-on work around 2031. I'd ask my father, who's a retired bricklayer, if I could work on sites with him on weekends. We'd stop eating out and I'd take any extra shifts at the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a punch. I'd be angry first, then afraid. I'd keep going in front of Lucia, but at night I'd be awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd cancel the big wedding. How would Lucia take that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say yes in a second, I think. She'd tell me she married me, not a party. That makes me feel worse in a way, because I wanted to give her the day she dreamed of.

say: I'd say it's **crazy**, and politicians should have had plans.
I'd tell Mr Pryce (my boss) he has two years to decide **what Ridgeway is**.
think: My job is gone within two years, because a machine does **buying for nothing**.
There is only **one other wholesaler**, so I would have nowhere to go.
do: Shrink the wedding to a **registry office** service, saving about 8,000.
Start learning **plumbing**, since robots reach hands-on work around 2031.
Work **weekends on sites** with my father and take extra shifts at the yard.
feel: Like a **punch**, then fear at night while I stay strong in front of Lucia.
S2.quote: I'd move the wedding to a small registry office service with just family, which saves about 8,000.
fieldNote: Reacts by cutting the **wedding**, his biggest planned expense.
Blames politicians, not tech firms, in line with a market view.
Hides distress from his fiancée and works overnight in his head.

steps.text: Move the wedding to a small registry office with just family
Start a plumbing course on weekday evenings
Work weekends on building sites with my father
Stop eating out and take extra yard shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it gives us a real window and we should use it. At work I'd tell Mr Pryce we should train staff on the tools and agree what comes next for each role. To friends I'd say start learning something new now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk job lasts three or four years and then I'm out, but five years is enough to switch. I'd rather go sideways into site management than start from scratch. The thin savings are still the problem, because training costs money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding but small, and put the rest into savings, aiming for three months by next summer. I'd take a part-time course in construction management, which costs about 1,500. I'd use the AI tools to get faster at my current job, so I look valuable while I train. By year three I'd apply for a site manager trainee job with a builder, because I know the materials better than most of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long hill, but one I can climb. I'd be less alarmed than with the two-year one, and more determined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for the wedding and for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You'd go from buyer to site manager. Why that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Pryce?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's where the decisions still need someone on the ground. A manager has to see the weather, the crew and the delivery, and I know materials. I'd want a job where my dad would say, you've got a trade, not just a desk.

say: I'd say five years is a **real window**, so we should use it.
I'd tell Mr Pryce to **train staff** and agree what comes next for each role.
think: My desk job lasts three or four years, but five is enough to **switch**.
The thin savings are the problem, because **training costs money**.
do: Keep a small wedding and save **three months** of expenses by next summer.
Take a part-time **construction management** course costing about 1,500.
Apply for a **site manager trainee** job by year three.
feel: A **long hill** I can climb, with more determination than fear.
S3.quote: A manager has to see the weather, the crew and the delivery, and I know materials.
fieldNote: Picks a **bridge career** that uses his product knowledge.
Wants his father's approval: a trade, not just a desk.
Still anxious because training money is short.

steps.text: Save three months of expenses by next summer
Take a part-time construction management course
Apply for site manager trainee jobs with builders by year three
Use AI tools to speed up buying while I train

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's time for the country to get it right, with apprenticeships and sensible rules. At work I'd tell Mr Pryce to start bringing in younger staff now so the skills are passed on. To friends I'd say get married, get a house, and keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fairly safe for a while. Ten years lets me pay off my loans and plan a family before things move. But I still want a second string to my bow, in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding goes ahead next summer as planned, though modest. Within three years I'd build six months of savings, and we'd start saving for a deposit on a house. I'd study evenings for a construction management diploma, and use AI a bit more at work each year. We'd hope to have our first child around year five, if the money looks right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels settled, even good. I still count pennies today, but the long runway lets me think about children and a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What do you picture for 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd keep learning. What would a typical year look like?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you and Lucia want to get done first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One course a year, and one new tool a year. Small steps that don't scare Lucia (my fiancée) or my boss. Last year I tried an AI helper for supplier emails, and next I'd try one for price forecasts.

say: I'd say ten years is time to get **apprenticeships** and sensible rules in place.
I'd tell friends to **get married**, buy a house and keep learning.
think: I'd feel **fairly safe** for a while, with time to pay off loans.
I still want a **second string** to my bow.
do: Build **six months** of savings within three years and start a house deposit.
Study evenings for a **construction management** diploma.
feel: **Settled**, even good, though I still count pennies today.
S4.quote: One course a year, and one new tool a year. Small steps that don't scare Lucia (my fiancée) or my boss.
fieldNote: Long timelines let him think about **children and a house**.
Steady habit: one course and one tool a year.
Remains uneasy because savings are still thin today.

steps.text: Hold the wedding next summer on a modest budget
Build six months of savings and start a house deposit
Study evenings for a construction management diploma
Try one new AI tool at work each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. There's no time to learn a trade, and the wedding would be wrecked. What would help is a hard notice period from employers, real apprenticeships with pay, and a decent chance to train without going into debt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that people shouldn't just wait for someone to sort it out. Work is how I've been raised to see myself, and if a machine does it all, I'd still need a reason to get up. I'd want to be useful to Lucia and to my family.

headlineQuote: Work is how I've been raised to see myself, and if a machine does it all, I'd still need a reason to get up.
portrait: Ben is a 27-year-old lead buyer at a **timber and building supplies** wholesaler, engaged to a primary school teacher.
He has under a month saved, lower pay than he expects, and a **wedding** to pay for.
He is traditional, believes in work and apprenticeships over handouts, and uses **AI now and then**.
In the fast AGI worlds he cuts the wedding and heads for a **trade** or site management.
He hides **money worry** from his fiancée and plans quietly.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries him most, with no time to learn a trade and a wedding at risk.
whatWouldHelp: A hard **notice period**, paid apprenticeships, and training without debt.
